Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Handling Events
Handling Events from Smart Contracts
Learn how events let your frontend and services react to on-chain activity with efficiency and history.
In this lesson

Understand event logs, subscribe to live events with Web3.js, query historical events, and parse indexed parameters for efficient filtering.

Why it matters

Events decouple UI updates from heavy polling. They reduce network traffic, provide near real-time updates, and give a verifiable history of contract activity.

Quick preview

We will add a CounterChanged event to a Counter contract, read historical events with getPastEvents, and listen for real-time events with contract.events.

Emit
Contract emits event into transaction log
Log
Event stored in transaction receipt logs for history
Subscribe
Web3.js listens and your UI reacts in near real-time
Explore Key Topics
Real-time subscriptions
contract.events.MyEvent() and on('data') handlers for live updates.
Historical queries
contract.getPastEvents() with fromBlock and indexed filters.
Indexed parameters
Use indexed keyword to enable efficient filtering by topics.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map directly to practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the purpose of smart contract events: what they record and why they are more efficient than continuous polling. That includes recognizing event logs in a transaction receipt and how events support external tools. Second, you'll learn to subscribe to real-time events using the contract. events interface in Web3. js so your UI can react as soon as a new block contains an event. Third, you will retrieve past events using getPastEvents and use fromBlock and toBlock to reconstruct historical state or audit activity. Finally, you will parse event data, distinguishing indexed parameters that can be filtered at the node level from non-indexed data that must be inspected client-side. Each objective includes a short example so you can connect the skill to the lab: for example, adding a CounterChanged event to a Counter contract and reading it from a frontend. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls: forgetting fromBlock when querying history, relying on non-indexed filters, or using the wrong provider type for subscriptions. These objectives prepare you to build responsive, efficient dApps that react to contract activity.

screens.title: Practical Skills You'll Apply
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond understanding and subscribing, you will practice additional operational skills that matter when building durable dApps. First, learn to choose an appropriate provider: WebSocket providers give persistent connections ideal for real-time subscriptions, while HTTP providers may rely on polling and can introduce latency. Second, implement robust handlers for on('changed') and on('error') events so your app responds correctly to chain reorganizations or network failures. Third, adopt lifecycle management: unsubscribe when components unmount to prevent memory leaks in long-running frontends. Fourth, combine getPastEvents with indexed filters to efficiently load initial state and then switch to live subscriptions for ongoing updates. Each of these is demonstrated in the Counter lab where you'll add a CounterChanged event, fetch past events to build the initial view, then listen for new increments. A common misconception is thinking filters work for any parameter; remember only indexed parameters can be filtered efficiently at the node level. These practical skills keep your app responsive, efficient, and resilient.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Practical Skills
Choose provider
WebSocketProvider is preferred for stable, low-latency subscriptions. HttpProvider can work but may rely on long polling.
Handle reorganizations
Listen for on('changed') to detect when an event is removed because of a chain reorg and re-sync state if needed.
Unsubscribe and lifecycle
Detach listeners when components unmount to avoid memory leaks in UIs that mount and unmount frequently.
Use indexed filters
Filters in getPastEvents operate on indexed event parameters; non-indexed fields must be filtered client-side.
Combine history and live
Fetch past events to build initial UI state, then subscribe for live events to keep the view current without polling.
Common mistake

Setting fromBlock too high or omitting it can cause you to miss important historical events.

screens.title: Why events instead of polling
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the contract's mechanism for broadcasting meaningful changes to the outside world. Instead of your frontend continuously calling view functions to check for updates, events let the node push notifications only when a relevant transaction is mined. That saves network requests and C P U on both client and node, and yields more immediate UI updates. A concrete example: imagine a deposit event emitted each time funds arrive. If you polled the balance every five seconds you would make many redundant calls when no deposit happened. If the contract emits a Deposit event, your app can update immediately on receipt and avoid repeated calls. An important distinction is that events are written to transaction receipt logs, not contract storage; they are efficient for external consumption but are not a substitute for on-chain state that must be read within contracts. A common misconception is assuming events are reliable storage; while they are durable in logs, they are meant for external indexing and can be affected by rare reorganizations. To handle that, subscribe to on('changed') notifications and re-fetch authoritative state when needed. When designing your dApp, use events for reactive UI and maintain occasional verification via direct calls for final consistency.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Events are push notifications stored in transaction logs; they reduce polling and give external apps a lightweight history of contract activity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Why events
Why events are efficient
Events are recorded in a transaction's receipt log so external tools can find them without reading contract storage or calling view functions repeatedly.
  • • Events are push-based: receive updates only when something happens.
  • • They reduce redundant network traffic compared with frequent polling.
  • • Events are ideal for UI updates, analytics, and off-chain workflows.
Key takeaway

Prefer events for notifications and UI reactivity, but validate critical state with occasional direct calls.

Analogy / Example
Think of events as email notifications: you receive one when something relevant happens rather than constantly checking the inbox.
Scenario

A dApp wants to update a balance display when a deposit occurs. The contract emits a Deposit event with the amount and sender. The frontend subscribes and updates immediately. If it polled, it would waste requests when no deposit occurred.

Common mistake
Treating events as in-contract storage: events are logs for external use and shouldn't be relied on by on-chain logic.
Pro tip
Fetch past events for initial state, then switch to subscriptions for live updates to avoid race conditions.

screens.title: Emitting events in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: In Solidity you declare an event and then call emit within a function to log values into the transaction receipt. Events are declared like a typed signature that lists parameters and which of them are indexed. For example, a storage contract might declare an event with a number and an indexed sender address. When a function stores a new value, it emits that event so off-chain tools can see the new data and who triggered it. Indexed parameters are stored in topics and enable efficient filtering when querying past events. Non-indexed parameters live in the event's data field and need to be inspected client-side. A concrete code example is included on the screen; read it to see the event declaration followed by emit inside store. A common misconception is thinking emit writes to contract state; it doesn't. Another subtlety is that the types in the event appear as stringified or numeric values in returnValues when accessed via Web3. js, so you will often parse integers or use a BigNumber library for large numeric types. After emitting, the event appears in the transaction receipt log and can be fetched with getPastEvents or received live by a subscription.

keyIdea.title: Emit usage
keyIdea.text: Declare event signatures in Solidity and call emit to append a record to the transaction receipt log for off-chain consumers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Emitting events
Solidity example
Event declaration and emit inside a function.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Storage {
    uint256 public data;
    event DataStored(uint256 newData, address indexed sender);

    function store(uint256 _data) public {
        data = _data;
        emit DataStored(_data, msg.sender);
    }
}
Notes & parsing
  • • The indexed keyword marks parameters stored in topics enabling node-side filtering.
  • • Non-indexed parameters are placed into the event's data blob and must be read from returnValues.
  • • When consumed via Web3.js numeric types may be stringified and require parsing or BigNumber handling.
Misconception
Emitting an event does not change contract storage; it records an off-chain-friendly log entry.
Example takeaway

Use indexed where you expect to filter often, otherwise include data for full context in the event payload.

screens.title: Indexed vs Non-indexed parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Events can include indexed parameters that become topics and non-indexed parameters that live in the data field. Indexed parameters are powerful because the node can filter by them directly when you call getPastEvents with a filter. For example, when an event includes an indexed sender address, you can query only events for that address without downloading every event and filtering client-side. Non-indexed fields are not filterable at the node level and require fetching a larger set of events then performing client-side filtering, which is inefficient for large histories. A concrete scenario: an NFT Transfer event commonly indexes from, to, and tokenId so marketplaces can quickly fetch transfers for a wallet. A common mistake is indexing too many fields or indexing complex types; remember you have a limited number of indexed topics and indexing has gas costs. Use indexed parameters for values you'll query frequently—addresses, IDs—and keep larger contextual data non-indexed. End by asking: which fields in your contract are queried often enough to justify indexing? Indexed vs Non-indexed parameters means index parameters you will query often; otherwise store them as non-indexed data and filter client-side when necessary.. In practical terms, how to decide which fields to index for efficient queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Index parameters you will query often; otherwise store them as non-indexed data and filter client-side when necessary.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Indexed vs Non-indexed
Indexed parameters
Stored in topics and searchable by the node. Use them for addresses and IDs you will filter on.
Non-indexed parameters
Stored in the data field; must be retrieved and filtered client-side if you need them.
When to index
Index when you'll query that field frequently from getPastEvents.
When not to index
Do not index large structs or rarely queried values; index count is limited.
Concrete example
An ERC-721 Transfer event typically indexes from, to, and tokenId so you can efficiently find tokens transferred to a user by filtering the to topic.
Common mistake
Trying to filter non-indexed fields at the node level. That requires fetching all events then filtering locally, which is inefficient at scale.
Check

Which event fields in your contract will you query often enough to index?

screens.title: Retrieving past events with getPastEvents
screens.narratorSegment: getPastEvents lets your app fetch historical occurrences of a contract event within a block range. Use fromBlock to set the earliest block to search and toBlock to cap the search; setting fromBlock to zero or the contract deployment block ensures a full history. You can include a filter object that selects indexed parameters, letting the node return only matching logs without client-side filtering. A typical flow is to call getPastEvents during application initialization to reconstruct the UI's initial state, then switch to a live subscription for continuing updates. For example, call getPastEvents('DataStored', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest', filter: { sender: '0xUser' } }) to fetch emissions for a specific indexed sender. Beware of a common pitfall: forgetting fromBlock or using a too-recent starting block can make you miss earlier events. Also remember that filtering by non-indexed fields is not supported at the node level; you must fetch results and then filter them client-side, which can be slow for large datasets. After retrieving events, examine event. returnValues to access parameters, parsing numeric strings into integers as needed. This method gives you a faithful historical view that you can combine with real-time subscriptions for a robust frontend.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › getPastEvents
JavaScript example
const past = await storageContract.getPastEvents('DataStored', {
  fromBlock: 0,
  toBlock: 'latest',
  // filter: { sender: "0x..." } // indexes only
});

past.forEach(ev => {
  console.log(ev.blockNumber, ev.returnValues.newData, ev.returnValues.sender);
});
Filter only accepts indexed parameters efficiently. Use fromBlock carefully to avoid missing events.
Practical steps
  • • Choose a fromBlock for the earliest relevant event (0 or deployment block).
  • • Use indexed filters for addresses or IDs whenever possible.
  • • Parse numeric return values; they may be strings in Web3.js.
Pitfall

Filtering by non-indexed fields requires fetching many events and filtering locally — this can be slow.

screens.title: Subscribing to real-time events
screens.narratorSegment: Subscribing to real-time events in Web3. js is achieved with contract. events. EventName and registering handlers for 'data', 'changed', and 'error' notifications. The typical pattern is to set up the listener when your application or component starts, react inside the data handler by updating UI or triggering workflows, and then remove the listener when your component unmounts. For example, on the DataStored event you will handle an incoming event object that includes event name, block number, transaction hash, and returnValues with parameters. Use on('changed') to detect when an event is removed due to a chain reorganization and then re-sync authoritative state or warn the user. Errors in the connection should be handled by on('error'), and reconnection logic is a practical necessity for production systems. Concrete example: set up storageContract. events. DataStored(). on('data', ev => { parse and update UI }). on('changed', ch => { handle reorg }). on('error', e => { reconnect or log }). A common misconception is that subscription guarantees permanence; events can be temporarily present then removed by a reorg. Always combine subscriptions with occasional verification via direct calls to the contract's view functions for final consistency.

keyIdea.title: Real-time pattern
keyIdea.text: Set up contract.events listeners with handlers for data, changed, and error, and manage lifecycle to avoid leaks and stale views.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Subscribe
Subscription handlers
Register these handlers on your subscription:
  • • on('data'): receives confirmed events; update UI or trigger tasks here.
  • • on('changed'): handles events removed by chain reorganizations; re-sync state.
  • • on('error'): handle provider or subscription errors and reconnect if needed.
Lifecycle
Create on mount, unsubscribe on unmount to prevent memory leaks in UIs.
Example pattern
storageContract.events.DataStored()
  .on('data', event => { /* parse event.returnValues and update UI */ })
  .on('changed', changed => { /* handle reorg: re-fetch authoritative state */ })
  .on('error', err => { /* reconnect or log error */ });
Remember to prefer a WebSocket provider for low-latency live subscriptions when available.

screens.title: Provider choice, reorgs and memory management
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right provider and designing listeners carefully are essential for production dApps. WebSocket providers maintain a persistent connection that delivers events with lower latency and fewer missed messages, making them the typical choice for real-time subscriptions. HTTP providers can provide event data via polling but often introduce delays and higher request volume. In addition to provider selection, design for rare but consequential events like blockchain reorganizations. When a reorg happens, an event you previously received can be removed; on('changed') notifies you so you can re-fetch authoritative state via a view call or mark the UI as uncertain until resolved. Finally, manage listener lifecycle: unsubscribing when a component unmounts prevents memory leaks in single-page applications. If you open many listeners and never close them, the process will accumulate event handlers and consume memory. A concrete mitigation is to store the subscription object returned by contract. events and call unsubscribe or detach listeners during cleanup. The misconception to avoid is assuming the node will always keep the same logs forever; design to detect and respond to changes so your application stays consistent.

Provider types
WebSocketProvider: persistent and low-latency. HttpProvider: may use polling and introduce latency.
Handle reorgs
on('changed') notifies you if an event is removed. Re-fetch authoritative state when that happens.
Memory management
Unsubscribe listeners on unmount to prevent growing handler counts and memory leaks in long-lived apps.
Example cleanup pattern
Save the subscription and call unsubscribe during teardown. Reconnect logic should back off to avoid tight retry loops on failures.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Counter Lab
Counter.sol (update)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    uint256 public count;

    event CounterChanged(uint256 newCount, address indexed sender);

    constructor() { count = 0; }

    function increment() public {
        count++;
        emit CounterChanged(count, msg.sender);
    }

    function decrement() public {
        count--;
        emit CounterChanged(count, msg.sender);
    }
}

fullNarratorScript:
Smart contracts emit events as a compact, historical record that external applications can consume. In this lesson you will learn why events are preferable to continuous polling, how Solidity emits logs into a transaction receipt, and how Web3. js exposes both real-time subscriptions and historical queries. We'll use a small Counter contract lab to practice emitting events, querying past events, and setting up a real-time listener that reacts when the counter changes. You will also see how indexed parameters let you filter efficiently, why a WebSocket provider is usually better for live updates, and how to guard against rare blockchain reorganizations. By the end of this chapter you will be able to decide when to use events, implement listeners that update a frontend, and recover or re-sync state when an event is removed by a chain reorg. A concrete example you will follow shows adding a CounterChanged event that reports the new count and the sender address, then using getPastEvents to reconstruct history and contract. events to receive live notifications. Throughout, watch for common mistakes like relying only on non-indexed filters or forgetting to unsubscribe — these can cost you latency or memory. How will you use events to make your dApp more responsive?

These learning objectives map directly to practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the purpose of smart contract events: what they record and why they are more efficient than continuous polling. That includes recognizing event logs in a transaction receipt and how events support external tools. Second, you'll learn to subscribe to real-time events using the contract. events interface in Web3. js so your UI can react as soon as a new block contains an event. Third, you will retrieve past events using getPastEvents and use fromBlock and toBlock to reconstruct historical state or audit activity. Finally, you will parse event data, distinguishing indexed parameters that can be filtered at the node level from non-indexed data that must be inspected client-side. Each objective includes a short example so you can connect the skill to the lab: for example, adding a CounterChanged event to a Counter contract and reading it from a frontend. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls: forgetting fromBlock when querying history, relying on non-indexed filters, or using the wrong provider type for subscriptions. These objectives prepare you to build responsive, efficient dApps that react to contract activity.

Beyond understanding and subscribing, you will practice additional operational skills that matter when building durable dApps. First, learn to choose an appropriate provider: WebSocket providers give persistent connections ideal for real-time subscriptions, while HTTP providers may rely on polling and can introduce latency. Second, implement robust handlers for on('changed') and on('error') events so your app responds correctly to chain reorganizations or network failures. Third, adopt lifecycle management: unsubscribe when components unmount to prevent memory leaks in long-running frontends. Fourth, combine getPastEvents with indexed filters to efficiently load initial state and then switch to live subscriptions for ongoing updates. Each of these is demonstrated in the Counter lab where you'll add a CounterChanged event, fetch past events to build the initial view, then listen for new increments. A common misconception is thinking filters work for any parameter; remember only indexed parameters can be filtered efficiently at the node level. These practical skills keep your app responsive, efficient, and resilient.

Events are the contract's mechanism for broadcasting meaningful changes to the outside world. Instead of your frontend continuously calling view functions to check for updates, events let the node push notifications only when a relevant transaction is mined. That saves network requests and C P U on both client and node, and yields more immediate UI updates. A concrete example: imagine a deposit event emitted each time funds arrive. If you polled the balance every five seconds you would make many redundant calls when no deposit happened. If the contract emits a Deposit event, your app can update immediately on receipt and avoid repeated calls. An important distinction is that events are written to transaction receipt logs, not contract storage; they are efficient for external consumption but are not a substitute for on-chain state that must be read within contracts. A common misconception is assuming events are reliable storage; while they are durable in logs, they are meant for external indexing and can be affected by rare reorganizations. To handle that, subscribe to on('changed') notifications and re-fetch authoritative state when needed. When designing your dApp, use events for reactive UI and maintain occasional verification via direct calls for final consistency.

In Solidity you declare an event and then call emit within a function to log values into the transaction receipt. Events are declared like a typed signature that lists parameters and which of them are indexed. For example, a storage contract might declare an event with a number and an indexed sender address. When a function stores a new value, it emits that event so off-chain tools can see the new data and who triggered it. Indexed parameters are stored in topics and enable efficient filtering when querying past events. Non-indexed parameters live in the event's data field and need to be inspected client-side. A concrete code example is included on the screen; read it to see the event declaration followed by emit inside store. A common misconception is thinking emit writes to contract state; it doesn't. Another subtlety is that the types in the event appear as stringified or numeric values in returnValues when accessed via Web3. js, so you will often parse integers or use a BigNumber library for large numeric types. After emitting, the event appears in the transaction receipt log and can be fetched with getPastEvents or received live by a subscription.

Events can include indexed parameters that become topics and non-indexed parameters that live in the data field. Indexed parameters are powerful because the node can filter by them directly when you call getPastEvents with a filter. For example, when an event includes an indexed sender address, you can query only events for that address without downloading every event and filtering client-side. Non-indexed fields are not filterable at the node level and require fetching a larger set of events then performing client-side filtering, which is inefficient for large histories. A concrete scenario: an NFT Transfer event commonly indexes from, to, and tokenId so marketplaces can quickly fetch transfers for a wallet. A common mistake is indexing too many fields or indexing complex types; remember you have a limited number of indexed topics and indexing has gas costs. Use indexed parameters for values you'll query frequently—addresses, IDs—and keep larger contextual data non-indexed. End by asking: which fields in your contract are queried often enough to justify indexing? Indexed vs Non-indexed parameters means index parameters you will query often; otherwise store them as non-indexed data and filter client-side when necessary.. getPastEvents lets your app fetch historical occurrences of a contract event within a block range. Use fromBlock to set the earliest block to search and toBlock to cap the search; setting fromBlock to zero or the contract deployment block ensures a full history. You can include a filter object that selects indexed parameters, letting the node return only matching logs without client-side filtering. A typical flow is to call getPastEvents during application initialization to reconstruct the UI's initial state, then switch to a live subscription for continuing updates. For example, call getPastEvents('DataStored', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest', filter: { sender: '0xUser' } }) to fetch emissions for a specific indexed sender. Beware of a common pitfall: forgetting fromBlock or using a too-recent starting block can make you miss earlier events. Also remember that filtering by non-indexed fields is not supported at the node level; you must fetch results and then filter them client-side, which can be slow for large datasets. After retrieving events, examine event. returnValues to access parameters, parsing numeric strings into integers as needed. This method gives you a faithful historical view that you can combine with real-time subscriptions for a robust frontend.

Subscribing to real-time events in Web3. js is achieved with contract. events. EventName and registering handlers for 'data', 'changed', and 'error' notifications. The typical pattern is to set up the listener when your application or component starts, react inside the data handler by updating UI or triggering workflows, and then remove the listener when your component unmounts. For example, on the DataStored event you will handle an incoming event object that includes event name, block number, transaction hash, and returnValues with parameters. Use on('changed') to detect when an event is removed due to a chain reorganization and then re-sync authoritative state or warn the user. Errors in the connection should be handled by on('error'), and reconnection logic is a practical necessity for production systems. Concrete example: set up storageContract. events. DataStored(). on('data', ev => { parse and update UI }). on('changed', ch => { handle reorg }). on('error', e => { reconnect or log }). A common misconception is that subscription guarantees permanence; events can be temporarily present then removed by a reorg. Always combine subscriptions with occasional verification via direct calls to the contract's view functions for final consistency.

Choosing the right provider and designing listeners carefully are essential for production dApps. WebSocket providers maintain a persistent connection that delivers events with lower latency and fewer missed messages, making them the typical choice for real-time subscriptions. HTTP providers can provide event data via polling but often introduce delays and higher request volume. In addition to provider selection, design for rare but consequential events like blockchain reorganizations. When a reorg happens, an event you previously received can be removed; on('changed') notifies you so you can re-fetch authoritative state via a view call or mark the UI as uncertain until resolved. Finally, manage listener lifecycle: unsubscribing when a component unmounts prevents memory leaks in single-page applications. If you open many listeners and never close them, the process will accumulate event handlers and consume memory. A concrete mitigation is to store the subscription object returned by contract. events and call unsubscribe or detach listeners during cleanup. The misconception to avoid is assuming the node will always keep the same logs forever; design to detect and respond to changes so your application stays consistent.
